column2: From Abū Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “Allah is Good and accepts only what is good.
Allah the Exalted has commanded the believers with what He commanded the messengers, saying: ‘O messengers, eat of the good things and do righteous deeds’ [al-Muʾminūn 23:51];
and the Exalted said: ‘O you who believe, eat of the good things We have provided for you’ [al-Baqarah 2:172].” Then he mentioned a man who travels far, dishevelled and dusty,

stretching out his hands to the sky: “O Lord! O Lord!” — while his food is unlawful, his drink is unlawful, his clothing is unlawful, and he has been nourished on the unlawful; “so how could he be answered?” Reported by Muslim.
Muslim recorded this hadith in the narration of Fuḍayl ibn Marzūq, from ʿAdī ibn Thābit, from Abū Ḥāzim, from Abū Hurayrah; al-Tirmidhī also recorded it and said: good (ḥasan) and unusual (gharīb).
Fuḍayl ibn Marzūq is reliable, of middling standing; Muslim recorded from him, but al-Bukhārī did not.

His words ﷺ, “Allah the Exalted is Good”: this has also come in the hadith of Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: “Allah is Good and loves what is good, Clean and loves cleanliness, Generous and loves generosity.”
Al-Tirmidhī recorded it, and its chain has been criticised. “Good” (ṭayyib) here means pure.

The meaning is that He, the Exalted, is holy and free of all deficiencies and faults. This is as in His words: “Good women are for good men, and good men for good women; they are innocent of what people say” [al-Nūr 24:26] — meaning those who are free of the filth and stains of indecency.

His words, “accepts only what is good”: the same meaning has come in the hadith on charity, whose wording is: “No one gives in charity from good earnings — and Allah accepts only what is good…” What is meant is that He, the Exalted, accepts only charity that is good and lawful.

It has been said that what is meant by his words “Allah accepts only what is good” in the hadith we are now discussing is more general than that: that He accepts only deeds that are good and pure of everything that corrupts them,
such as showing off and self-admiration, and only wealth that is good and lawful. For goodness is a quality of deeds, words and beliefs, and all of these divide into good and foul.
It has been said that all of this is included in His words, the Exalted: “Say: The foul and the good are not equal, even though the abundance of the foul may impress you” [al-Māʾidah 5:100].

Allah the Exalted divided speech into good and foul, saying: “Allah has struck a parable: a good word is like a good tree” [Ibrāhīm 14:24], and “The parable of a foul word is that of a foul tree” [Ibrāhīm 14:26]; and the Exalted said: “To Him ascends the good word” [Fāṭir 35:10]. And He described the Messenger ﷺ as one who makes good things lawful and foul things unlawful [al-Aʿrāf 7:157].

It has been said that deeds, words and beliefs are included in that too. Allah the Exalted described the believers as good, in His words, the Exalted: “those whom the angels take in death while they are good” [al-Naḥl 16:32]. At death the angels say: Come out, O good soul that was in a good body;

and on their entering Paradise the angels greet them and say to them: “You have been good, so enter it to abide for ever” [al-Zumar 39:73]. It has come in a hadith that when a believer visits a brother of his for the sake of Allah, the angels say to him: “You have been good, good has been your walking, and you have taken up a dwelling in Paradise.”

The believer, then, is good through and through — his heart, his tongue and his body — by the faith that dwells in his heart, the remembrance that appears on his tongue and the righteous deeds that appear on his limbs, which are the fruit of faith and come under its name. All these good things Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, accepts.
One of the greatest things by which a believer's deeds become good is the goodness of his food — that it be lawful. By that his deeds are made pure.
This hadith indicates that deeds are accepted and made pure only by eating what is lawful, and that eating what is unlawful corrupts deeds and prevents their acceptance. For after establishing

that “Allah accepts only what is good,” he said that Allah has commanded the believers with what He commanded the messengers, saying: “O messengers, eat of the good things and do righteous deeds,” and saying: “O you who believe, eat of the good things We have provided for you.”

What is meant by this is that the messengers and their nations are commanded to eat of the good things, which are the lawful, and to do righteous deeds. So long as one's food is lawful, one's deeds are righteous and accepted; but if one's food is not lawful, how can one's deeds be accepted?

What he mentioned after that about supplication — how can it be accepted alongside the unlawful? — is an example illustrating how unlikely it is that deeds will be accepted when one is nourished on the unlawful.
Al-Ṭabarānī recorded, with a chain open to question, that Ibn ʿAbbās said: This verse was recited in the presence of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ:
“O people, eat of what is on earth, lawful and good” [al-Baqarah 2:168]. Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ stood up and said: O Messenger of Allah, ask Allah to make me one whose supplications are answered.
The Prophet ﷺ said: “O Saʿd, make your food good and you will be one whose supplications are answered.

By Him in whose hand is the soul of Muḥammad, the servant throws an unlawful morsel into his belly and Allah accepts no deed from him for forty days; and any servant whose flesh has grown from ill-gotten gain, the Fire is more fitting for him.”
In the Musnad of Imam Aḥmad, also with a chain open to question, Ibn ʿUmar said: “Whoever buys a garment for ten dirhams, one dirham of whose price is unlawful,
Allah will not accept any prayer from him as long as he wears it.” Then he put his two fingers in his ears and said: May they be deafened if I did not hear it from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.
Something with the same meaning is also narrated as marfūʿ (the Prophet's words) from the hadith of ʿAlī (may Allah be pleased with him); al-Bazzār and others recorded it with a very weak chain.

Al-Ṭabarānī recorded, with a chain that has some weakness, from the hadith of Abū Hurayrah, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “When a man sets out for Ḥajj with good provision, puts his foot in the stirrup and calls out, ‘Here I am at Your service, O Allah, here I am,’ a caller calls to him from the sky:

‘At your service and at your pleasure! Your provision is lawful, your mount is lawful, and your Ḥajj is accepted and free of sin.’ But when a man sets out with foul provision, puts his foot in the stirrup and calls out, ‘Here I am at Your service, O Allah, here I am,’ a caller calls to him from the sky: ‘Neither at your service nor at your pleasure! Your provision is unlawful, your spending is unlawful, and your Ḥajj is not accepted.’”
Something similar is narrated from the hadith of ʿUmar, also with a weak chain.
Abū Yaḥyā al-Qattāt narrated from Mujāhid that Ibn ʿAbbās said: Allah does not accept the prayer of a man with something unlawful in his belly.

Scholars have disagreed over someone who performs Ḥajj with unlawful wealth, or prays in an unlawful garment: is the obligation of prayer or Ḥajj discharged by it? There are two reported positions from Imam Aḥmad on this. The hadiths we have mentioned show that a deed is not accepted when one is involved with the unlawful.

But acceptance may mean being pleased with the deed, and praising its doer, commending him among the angels and taking pride in him; or it may mean obtaining reward and recompense for it; or it may mean that the obligation is discharged by it.

If acceptance here is meant in the first or the second sense, that does not prevent the obligation from being discharged by it — just as it has come that the prayer of a runaway slave is not accepted, nor that of a woman whose husband is angry with her, nor that of someone who goes to a soothsayer,

nor that of someone who drinks wine, for forty days. What is meant — and Allah knows best — is the denial of acceptance in the first or second sense; and that is what is meant — and Allah knows best — by His words, the Mighty and Majestic: “Allah accepts only from the God-fearing” [al-Māʾidah 5:27].
That is why this verse made the Salaf fear intensely for themselves: they feared that they might not be among the God-fearing from whom deeds are accepted.
Aḥmad was asked about the meaning of “the God-fearing” in it, and said: He guards against things, so that he does not fall into what is not lawful for him.

Abū ʿAbdillāh al-Nājī the ascetic (may Allah have mercy on him) said: Five qualities make a deed complete: faith, through knowing Allah, the Mighty and Majestic; knowing the truth; doing the deed sincerely for Allah;
acting according to the Sunnah; and eating what is lawful. If one of them is missing, the deed is not raised up. For if you know Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, but do not know the truth,
you do not benefit; if you know the truth but do not know Allah, you do not benefit; if you know Allah and know the truth but do not do the deed sincerely, you do not benefit;

if you know Allah, know the truth and do the deed sincerely, but not according to the Sunnah, you do not benefit; and if the four are complete but your food is not from what is lawful, you do not benefit.
Wuhayb ibn al-Ward said: Even if you stood as constantly as this pillar, nothing would benefit you until you looked at what enters your belly, whether it is lawful or unlawful.

As for charity given from unlawful wealth, it is not accepted, as in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim from Ibn ʿUmar, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Allah does not accept prayer without purification, nor charity from stolen spoils.”

In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, from Abū Hurayrah, the Prophet ﷺ said: “No one gives in charity from good earnings — and Allah accepts only what is good — but the All-Merciful takes it with His right hand,” and he mentioned the rest of the hadith.
In the Musnad of Imam Aḥmad, from Ibn Masʿūd, the Prophet ﷺ said: “No servant earns wealth unlawfully and spends from it and is blessed in it,

or gives it in charity and has it accepted from him; and he does not leave it behind him but it becomes his provision for the Fire. Allah does not erase evil with evil, but erases evil with good; the foul does not erase the foul.”

It is narrated from the hadith of Darrāj, from Ibn Ḥujayrah, from Abū Hurayrah, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Whoever earns wealth unlawfully and gives it in charity has no reward for it, and its burden is upon him.”
Ibn Ḥibbān recorded it in his Ṣaḥīḥ, and some narrated it as mawqūf (the words of Abū Hurayrah himself).
Among the mursal reports of al-Qāsim ibn Mukhaymirah: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

“Whoever acquires wealth through sin and uses it to maintain ties of kinship, or gives it in charity, or spends it in the way of Allah, Allah will gather it all together and then cast it into the fire of Hell.”
It is narrated that Abū al-Dardāʾ and Yazīd ibn Maysarah likened someone who acquires wealth unlawfully and gives it in charity to someone who takes an orphan's property and clothes a widow with it.

Ibn ʿAbbās was asked about someone who had held an office in which he did wrong and took what was unlawful, and then repented, and was now performing Ḥajj, freeing slaves and giving in charity from it. He said: The foul does not expiate the foul.

Ibn Masʿūd likewise said: The foul does not expiate the foul, but the good expiates the foul. Al-Ḥasan said: O you who give in charity to the poor man out of mercy for him, have mercy on the one you have wronged!
It should be understood that charity from unlawful wealth takes place in two ways.

The first is that the embezzler, the usurper or the like gives it in charity on his own behalf. This is what these hadiths mean in saying that it is not accepted from him: he is not rewarded for it, but on the contrary sins by disposing of another's property without his permission; nor does the owner gain any reward from it,

since he neither aimed at it nor intended it. This is what a number of scholars said, among them Ibn ʿAqīl of our school. In the book of ʿAbd al-Razzāq, in the narration of Zayd ibn al-Akhnas al-Khuzāʿī, he asked Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib: I have found a lost item; may I give it in charity?
He said: Neither you nor its owner will be rewarded.
Perhaps he meant giving it in charity before announcing it as one is required to.

If the ruler, or one of his deputies, takes from the public treasury what he is not entitled to, and gives charity from it, frees slaves, or builds a mosque or anything else from which people benefit, what is reported from Ibn ʿUmar is that he is like a usurper who gives in charity what he has usurped.
That is what he said to ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿĀmir, the governor of al-Baṣrah. People had gathered around him as he lay dying, praising him for his kindness and generosity,

while Ibn ʿUmar kept silent. He asked him to speak, and Ibn ʿUmar narrated to him the hadith “Allah does not accept charity from stolen spoils,” and then said to him: And you were governor of al-Baṣrah.

Asad ibn Mūsā said in Kitāb al-Waraʿ: al-Fuḍayl ibn ʿIyāḍ told us, from Manṣūr, from Tamīm ibn Salamah, who said: Ibn ʿĀmir said to ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar: What do you think of these mountain passes we make easy and these springs we cause to gush forth — is there reward for us in them?
Ibn ʿUmar said: Do you not know that the foul never expiates the foul?

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Ziyād told us, from Abū Malīḥ, from Maymūn ibn Mihrān, who said: Ibn ʿUmar said to Ibn ʿĀmir, when he asked him about freeing slaves: Your example is that of a man who stole a pilgrim's camels and then fought on them in the way of Allah; see whether it would be accepted from him!

Some of those who were strict in scrupulousness, such as Ṭāwūs and Wuhayb ibn al-Ward, avoided benefiting from what such kings had built. Imam Aḥmad (may Allah have mercy on him), however, allowed benefiting from the public works they made,

such as mosques, bridges and cisterns, for these are paid for from the fayʾ revenue — unless, that is, it is certain that they built something of the kind with unlawful money, such as illegal tolls, usurped property and the like;

in that case one avoids benefiting from what was made with the unlawful money. Perhaps Ibn ʿUmar objected only to their taking treasury funds for themselves and claiming that whatever they then did with them
was charity from them, for this resembles usurpation. The objection some scholars raised to kings building mosques is to be understood in the same way.

Abū al-Faraj ibn al-Jawzī said: I saw one of the earlier scholars asked about someone who earned lawful and unlawful money from sultans and governors and then built hospices (ribāṭs) and mosques: would he have a reward?
He gave a fatwa that would set the spender's heart at ease, saying that in endowing what he did not own he had a share like that of a broker,
since he did not know the identities of those whose property had been usurped so as to return it to them.
He said: I said: How astonishing that men set themselves up to give fatwas without knowing the foundations of the Sharīʿah! One should first look at the position of this spender. If he is a sultan,

the ways in which what comes out of the public treasury must be spent are known; how then can he deny it to those entitled to it and tie it up in something of no use, such as building a madrasah or a ribāṭ?
If he is one of the governors or the sultans' deputies, he must return what ought to be returned to the public treasury. If it is unlawful or usurped, every disposal of it is unlawful,

and he must return it to the person it was taken from or to his heirs. If that person is not known, it is returned to the public treasury, to be spent on public interests or on charity, and the one who took it gains nothing but sin. End of quotation.

His words concern only the sultans he knew in his own time, who denied those entitled to the fayʾ their rights and disposed of it for themselves as owners do, building madrasahs, ribāṭs and the like that they named after themselves and that may not even be needed,
and favouring some people with it over others. But suppose there were a just imam who gave people their rights from the fayʾ and then built for them from it what they needed — a mosque,
a madrasah, a hospital and the like: that would be permissible. And if someone who took money for himself from the public treasury built with what he took something that was needed, in circumstances

where building from the public treasury is permissible, but named it after himself, the case may be derived from the disagreement over a usurper who returns property to its owner by way of charity or gift: is he thereby released from liability or not?
All of this applies when building is done according to need, without extravagance or ornamentation.
ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ordered the mosque of al-Baṣrah to be repaired from the public treasury, and forbade them to go beyond the parts that had cracked,
saying: I find no right for building in the wealth of Allah. It is narrated that he said: The Muslims have no need of anything that harms their treasury.
Note that some scholars held that the disposal of another's property by a usurper and the like depends on the owner's ratification: if he ratifies it, it stands.
Some scholars of our school related a reported position of Aḥmad that if someone pays his zakāh from usurped property and the owner then ratifies it, it stands and the zakāh obligation is discharged.

Likewise Ibn Abī Mūsā derived a position from Aḥmad that if someone frees another person's slave on his own behalf, undertaking to pay compensation from his own wealth, and the owner then ratifies it, it stands

and the manumission takes effect; but this contradicts Aḥmad's explicit statement. It is reported of the Ḥanafīs that if someone usurped a sheep and slaughtered it for his tamattuʿ or qirān Ḥajj, and the owner then ratified it, it would count for him.

The second way in which a usurper may dispose of usurped property is to give it in charity on its owner's behalf when he cannot return it to him or to his heirs. This is permissible according to most scholars, among them
Mālik, Abū Ḥanīfah, Aḥmad and others.

Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr said: Al-Zuhrī, Mālik, al-Thawrī, al-Awzāʿī and al-Layth held that someone who has stolen from the spoils, when the army has dispersed and he cannot reach its members, should hand over a fifth of it to the imam
and give the rest in charity. This is narrated from ʿUbādah ibn al-Ṣāmit, Muʿāwiyah and al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, and it resembles the position of Ibn Masʿūd and Ibn ʿAbbās,

for they both held that wealth whose owner is unknown should be given in charity. He said: They agreed by consensus that a found item may be given in charity once it has been announced and there is no trace of its owner, and they held that if the owner comes he may choose between the reward and compensation; and the same applies to usurped property. End of quotation.
It is narrated that Mālik ibn Dīnār said: I asked ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abī Rabāḥ about someone who has unlawful wealth, does not know its owners and wants to be rid of it.
He said: He should give it in charity, but I do not say that this will be enough to clear him.
Mālik said: This statement of ʿAṭāʾ's was dearer to me than its weight in gold.
Sufyān said about someone who bought usurped goods from people: He should return them to them; if he cannot reach them, he gives all of it in charity and does not take back his capital.

He said the same about someone who sold something to a person with whom dealings are disliked because of doubts about his wealth: he should give the price in charity. Ibn al-Mubārak disagreed with him and said: He gives the profit alone in charity. Aḥmad said: He gives the profit in charity.

Aḥmad said the same about someone who inherited wealth from his father, whose father used to sell to people with whom dealings are disliked: he gives the amount of the profit in charity and takes the rest.
Something similar is narrated from a number of the Companions, among them ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb and ʿAbdullāh ibn Yazīd al-Anṣārī.
The well-known position of al-Shāfiʿī (may Allah have mercy on him) on unlawful wealth is that it is kept and not given in charity until the person entitled to it appears.

Al-Fuḍayl ibn ʿIyāḍ held that someone who has unlawful wealth whose owners he does not know should destroy it, throwing it into the sea, and not give it in charity, saying: One draws near to Allah only with what is good.
The correct view is that it is given in charity,

because destroying and wasting wealth is forbidden, and holding it back for ever exposes it to destruction and to seizure by oppressors. Nor is the charity given on behalf of the one who earned it, so that he would be seeking nearness to Allah with something foul;
it is charity on behalf of its owner, so that its benefit may reach him in the Hereafter, since he cannot benefit from it in this world.

His words: “Then he mentioned a man who travels far, dishevelled and dusty, stretching out his hands to the sky: ‘O Lord! O Lord!’ — while his food is unlawful, his drink is unlawful, his clothing is unlawful, and he has been nourished on the unlawful; so how could he be answered?”

In these words he ﷺ pointed to the etiquette of supplication, to the causes that bring about its being answered, and to what prevents its being answered. Among the causes that bring about the answering of supplication he mentioned four.
The first is travelling far. Travel by itself brings about the answering of supplication, as in the hadith of Abū Hurayrah, from the Prophet ﷺ:

“Three supplications are answered, without doubt: the supplication of the wronged, the supplication of the traveller, and the supplication of a parent for his child.” Abū Dāwūd, Ibn Mājah and al-Tirmidhī recorded it; al-Tirmidhī's version has “of a parent against his child”.
Something similar is narrated from Ibn Masʿūd as his own words.
The longer the journey, the closer it brings one to having supplication answered,
because it is a likely occasion for the soul to be humbled by long absence from home and by bearing hardships, and brokenness of heart is one of the greatest causes of supplication being answered.

The second is shabbiness of dress and appearance — being dishevelled and dusty. This too is among the things that bring about the answering of supplication, as in the well-known hadith from the Prophet ﷺ: “Many a dishevelled, dusty man in two worn garments, turned away from doors — if he swore by Allah, Allah would fulfil his oath.”
When the Prophet ﷺ went out to pray for rain, he went out in shabby clothes, humble and imploring.
Muṭarrif ibn ʿAbdullāh had a nephew who was imprisoned. He put on his old, worn clothes and took a staff in his hand. He was asked: What is this?
He said: I am humbling myself before my Lord, so that perhaps He will accept my intercession for my nephew.
The third is stretching out the hands to the sky. This is part of the etiquette of supplication through which one hopes it will be answered. In the hadith of Salmān, from the Prophet ﷺ:

“Allah the Exalted is Modest and Generous; He is too modest, when a man raises his hands to Him, to send them back empty and disappointed.” Imam Aḥmad, Abū Dāwūd, al-Tirmidhī and Ibn Mājah recorded it.
Something similar is narrated from the hadiths of Anas, Jābir and others.

The Prophet ﷺ used to raise his hands when praying for rain until the whiteness of his armpits could be seen, and on the day of Badr he raised his hands, asking for victory over the polytheists, until his cloak fell from his shoulders.

Various ways of raising the hands in supplication have been narrated from the Prophet ﷺ. One is that he would point with his index finger alone; it is narrated that he did this on the pulpit, and that he did it when he mounted his riding camel.
A number of scholars held that in the qunūt supplication in prayer one points with one's finger, among them al-Awzāʿī, Saʿīd ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz and Isḥāq ibn Rāhawayh.
Ibn ʿAbbās and others said: This is sincerity in supplication. Ibn Sīrīn said: When you praise Allah, point with one finger.
Another is that he ﷺ raised his hands with their backs towards the qiblah, while he was facing it, and their palms towards his face.
This form has been narrated from the Prophet ﷺ in the supplication for rain, and some recommended raising the hands in this form when praying for rain, among them al-Jūzajānī.
One of the Salaf said: Raising the hands in this way is imploring.

Another is the reverse of that. This too has been narrated from the Prophet ﷺ in praying for rain, and it is narrated that a number of the Salaf used to supplicate in this way. Some of them said that raising the hands in this way is seeking protection with Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and taking refuge in Him —
among them Ibn ʿUmar, Ibn ʿAbbās and Abū Hurayrah. It is narrated from the Prophet ﷺ that when he prayed for rain he raised his hands, and when he sought refuge he raised his hands in this way.
Another is raising the hands with the palms towards the sky and the backs towards the earth.

The command to do this when asking of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has come in more than one hadith, and it is narrated from Ibn ʿUmar, Abū Hurayrah and Ibn Sīrīn that this is supplication and asking of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.
Another is the reverse of that: turning the hands over, with their backs towards the sky and their palms towards the earth.
In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, from Anas: the Prophet ﷺ prayed for rain and pointed with the backs of his hands towards the sky.
Imam Aḥmad (may Allah have mercy on him) recorded it, and his wording is: “He spread out his hands and turned their backs towards the sky.”
Abū Dāwūd recorded it, and his wording is: He prayed for rain like this — that is, he stretched out his hands and turned their palms towards the earth.

Imam Aḥmad recorded from the hadith of Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī, who said: The Prophet ﷺ was standing at ʿArafah supplicating like this — and he raised his hands to the level of his chest, with the palms facing the earth.
Ḥammād ibn Salamah described the Prophet's raising of his hands at ʿArafah in the same way.
It is narrated from Ibn Sīrīn that this is seeking protection.
Al-Ḥumaydī said: This is earnest entreaty (ibtihāl).

The fourth is pressing Allah insistently by repeatedly invoking His lordship. This is one of the greatest means of seeking an answer to supplication. Al-Bazzār recorded from the hadith of ʿĀʾishah, as marfūʿ: “When the servant says ‘O Lord’ four times, Allah says: Here I am, My servant; ask and you will be given.”

Al-Ṭabarānī and others recorded from the hadith of Saʿd ibn Khārijah that some people complained to the Prophet ﷺ of drought, and he said: “Kneel down on your knees and say: O Lord, O Lord,” and he raised his index finger to the sky. They were given rain until they wished it would be lifted from them.
In the Musnad and elsewhere, from al-Faḍl ibn ʿAbbās, the Prophet ﷺ said: “Prayer is in twos, with a tashahhud in every two rakʿahs, and with imploring,

humility and lowliness, and lifting your hands” — he says: raising them to your Lord with their palms towards your face — “and saying: O Lord, O Lord. Whoever does not do that, his prayer is deficient.”
Yazīd al-Raqāshī reported that Anas said: No servant says “O Lord, O Lord, O Lord” but his Lord says to him: “Here I am, here I am.”
It is narrated that Abū al-Dardāʾ and Ibn ʿAbbās used to say: The greatest name of Allah is “Lord, Lord”.
ʿAṭāʾ said: No servant says “O Lord, O Lord, O Lord” three times but Allah looks upon him. This was mentioned to al-Ḥasan, and he said: Do you not read the Qurʾān?
Then he recited His words, the Exalted:

“Those who remember Allah standing, sitting and lying on their sides, and reflect on the creation of the heavens and the earth: ‘Our Lord, You did not create this in vain; glory be to You! So protect us from the punishment of the Fire. Our Lord, whoever You admit into the Fire You have disgraced, and the wrongdoers will have no helpers. Our Lord, we have heard a caller calling to faith, “Believe in your Lord,” and we have believed. Our Lord, forgive us our sins, wipe away our misdeeds and take us in death with the righteous. Our Lord, give us what You promised us through Your messengers, and do not disgrace us on the Day of Resurrection; You never break Your promise.’ And their Lord answered them: ‘I do not let the deed of any doer among you go to waste’” [Āl ʿImrān 3:191–195].

Whoever reflects on the supplications mentioned in the Qurʾān will find that they mostly begin with the name “Lord”, as in His words, the Exalted: “Our Lord, give us good in this world and good in the Hereafter, and protect us from the punishment of the Fire” [al-Baqarah 2:201];

“Our Lord, do not take us to task if we forget or err. Our Lord, do not lay upon us a burden like the one You laid upon those before us. Our Lord, do not burden us with what we have no strength to bear” [al-Baqarah 2:286]; and His words: “Our Lord, do not let our hearts swerve after You have guided us” [Āl ʿImrān 3:8].
There is much like this in the Qurʾān.
Mālik and Sufyān were asked about someone who says in supplication “O my Master”, and they said: He should say “O Lord”.
Mālik added: as the prophets said in their supplications.

As for what prevents supplication from being answered, he ﷺ indicated that it is indulging freely in the unlawful, in food, drink, clothing and nourishment. The hadith of Ibn ʿAbbās to this effect has already been mentioned,

in which the Prophet ﷺ said to Saʿd: “Make your food good and you will be one whose supplications are answered.” So eating, drinking and wearing what is lawful, and being nourished by it, is a cause that brings about the answering of supplication.
ʿIkrimah ibn ʿAmmār narrated: al-Aṣfar told us: Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ was asked: How is it that, of all the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, your supplications are the ones answered?
He said: I have never raised a morsel to my mouth without knowing where it came from and where it had come out of.
Wahb ibn Munabbih said: Whoever would like Allah to answer his supplication should make his food good. Sahl ibn ʿAbdullāh said:
Whoever eats what is lawful for forty days, his supplication is answered. Yūsuf ibn Asbāṭ said: It has reached us that a servant's supplication is held back from the heavens because of bad food.
His words ﷺ, “so how (annā) could he be answered?”, mean: in what way (kayfa) could he be answered?

It is a question expressing astonishment and how unlikely it is; it does not state outright that an answer is impossible or wholly ruled out. From this one learns that indulging in the unlawful and being nourished by it is one of the things that prevent an answer; but something may be present that keeps this obstacle from having its effect.

Committing forbidden acts may also prevent an answer, and so may abandoning obligations, as in the hadith that abandoning commanding right and forbidding wrong prevents the supplications of the good from being answered; while doing acts of obedience brings about the answering of supplication.

That is why, when the men who had entered the cave, and on whom the rock had closed, sought a means to Allah through their righteous deeds done sincerely for Allah the Exalted, and called upon Allah by them, their supplication was answered.
Wahb ibn Munabbih said: Someone who supplicates without deeds is like someone who shoots without a bowstring.
He also said: Righteous deeds carry supplication to its goal. Then he recited His words, the Exalted: “To Him ascends the good word, and righteous deeds raise it up” [Fāṭir 35:10].
ʿUmar said: It is through scrupulous avoidance of what Allah has forbidden that Allah accepts supplication and glorification.
Abū Dharr (may Allah be pleased with him) said: With righteousness, supplication is needed only as much as food needs salt.
Muḥammad ibn Wāsiʿ said: With scrupulousness, a little supplication is enough. Sufyān was asked: Why do you not supplicate to Allah?
He said: Leaving sins is supplication.

Al-Layth said: Mūsā (peace be upon him) saw a man raising his hands and asking Allah earnestly. Mūsā said: O my Lord, Your servant has called upon You until I have taken pity on him, and You are the Most Merciful of the merciful; what have You done about his need?
He said: O Mūsā, even if he raised his hands until he could go on no longer, I would not look into his need until he looks to My right.
Al-Ṭabarānī recorded something with the same meaning, with a weak chain, from Ibn ʿAbbās as marfūʿ.

Mālik ibn Dīnār said: An affliction befell the Children of Israel, and they went out [to pray]. Allah the Exalted revealed to their prophet: Tell them: You go out to the open ground with impure bodies,
and raise to Me hands with which you have shed blood and filled your houses with the unlawful. Now My anger against you has grown fierce, and you will only grow further from Me.
One of the Salaf said: Do not think the answer slow in coming when you have blocked its paths with sins. One poet took up this idea and said:
We call on our God in every distress, / then forget Him when the distress is lifted.
How can we hope for an answer to a prayer / whose path we have blocked with our sins?
